chunks: Why MOSFET gates fear overvoltage. The question: Why are MOSFETs sensitive to overvoltage conditions applied at the gate?
A MOSFET gate is a metal plate separated from the silicon by an extremely thin layer of glass (silicon dioxide).
That glass is a good insulator, but it is so thin that a modest voltage can break it. Once it breaks, the gate is permanently shorted and the transistor is dead.
Picture a sheet of ice over a pond. Thin ice holds a small weight with no problem, but there is a limit. Go past it and the ice cracks, and it never heals.
The oxide works the same way. The danger is made worse because the gate is like a tiny capacitor, a part that stores charge.
It has so little room for charge that a small bit of static makes a huge voltage.
With only 1 ohms in the loop the gate overshoots 12 volts by 60% (to about 19 volts), right up to the 20 volts rating; adding resistance damps it. Critical damping at about 6.
3 ohms gives a clean edge but slower switching.
Real gates also ring via source inductance that couples the drain current into V GS (common-source inductance), which is not included here.
Gate oxide: the thin glass layer under the gate. Breakdown: the permanent failure when the electric field is too strong. Electric field: voltage divided by thickness.
Thin oxide means a high field even at low voltage. ESD: electrostatic discharge, a brief static zap, such as from a fingertip.
Absolute maximum V GS : the datasheet limit you must never exceed.
Glass breaks at a field of roughly 10 MV/cm.
If the oxide is 5 nm thick, that is 5 times 10 to the -7 cm, so the breakdown voltage is about 10 to the 7 times 5 times 10 to the -7 equals 5 volts.
A 5 volts spike on a gate that thin is fatal.
So we add protection: a series resistor, a Zener (a diode that clamps the voltage at a set level) across gate and source, and a pull-down resistor so the gate is never left unconnected.
That is the whole idea.
"The gate is a capacitor with a very thin oxide, a few nanometers in logic and tens of nanometers in power FETs, so even a few volts makes a very high field.
Silicon dioxide breaks down at about 10 MV/cm and the damage is permanent, which is why V GS maximums are only around ±8 to ±20 volts.
Plus the gate has no DC path and tiny capacitance, so a small ESD charge gives hundreds of volts, and gate-loop ringing or Miller coupling can overshoot the drive.
I protect it with a gate resistor, a Zener clamp, a pull-down, and ESD diodes."
